analysis.one_liner: Requires online companies to protect personal data and stop selling or misusing it.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in December 2019 with 16 cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would hold companies that collect people's online data to duties similar to those doctors and lawyers owe their patients and clients: a duty to keep the data secure, a duty not to use it in ways that foreseeably harm the user, and a duty not to sell or share it with anyone who doesn't follow the same rules. It covers sensitive information like Social Security numbers, health records, biometric identifiers, and precise location. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet or any digital service. The bill would give users enforceable protections against data breaches, against their data being used in ways that foreseeably cause financial or physical harm, and against their data being sold to third parties that don't meet the same standards. It specifically protects sensitive information — Social Security numbers, health information, biometric data, precise geolocation, and private messages — with mandatory breach notification.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes three duties on online service providers: reasonably secure personal data from unauthorized access, refrain from using it in ways that cause foreseeable material physical or financial harm, and never disclose or sell it to anyone not bound by the same duties.
Requires prompt notification to users whose sensitive data is breached, with the FTC able to extend notification requirements to other data categories by regulation.

Defines sensitive data broadly to include Social Security numbers, children's information, financial account numbers, biometric identifiers, precise geolocation, health information, and private user content.

Lets the FTC and state attorneys general enforce the duties as FTC Act violations, with state suits allowed to seek civil penalties calculated per day of violation or per harmed user, and extends FTC jurisdiction to nonprofits and common carriers that would otherwise be exempt.
Prohibits companies from making users waive these rights in terms of service or any other contract.

analysis.who_pays: Online companies, advertising platforms, and data brokers that profit from collecting and monetizing personal data. They would bear compliance costs and lose some ability to sell or reuse data, and those costs could be partly passed on through advertising prices or paid services.

drawbacks.text: There is no private right of action: individual users could not sue companies directly; enforcement depends entirely on the FTC and state attorneys general, which could leave many violations unaddressed.
Mandatory breach notification applies only to sensitive data at first; for other data, notification depends on future FTC rulemaking.
The FTC may exempt categories of providers based on size, complexity, and cost-benefit factors, which could narrow coverage for small businesses but also open the door to carve-outs.
Compliance and security costs would fall on companies of every size that collect personal data, and some of that cost could be passed to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address real, widespread harms — breaches of health, financial, and location data, and data uses that users never agreed to. The main design weakness is that individuals have no direct right to sue, so the law's strength depends on active FTC and state enforcement. Compliance costs are real but proportionate to the value companies extract from personal data, and the bill lets the FTC scale obligations to company size.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in December 2019 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, it never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the Data Care Act of 2019 on December 2, 2019, joined by 16 original cosponsors.
All 16 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican signed on to the bill.
The same day it was introduced, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action appears in the bill's history — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online platforms, advertisers, and data brokers kept collecting, using, and selling personal data with no new federal duties of care or loyalty, and the status quo of FTC-only, case-by-case privacy enforcement continued.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Hawaii; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Data Care Act of 2019 establishing duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality for online service providers.

for.name: 16 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors (15 Democrats and 1 Independent, including Sens. Sanders, Klobuchar, Booker, Durbin, Brown, and Markey)

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral; the bill died in this committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 2, 2019 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the remainder of the 116th Congress.

against.name: Sen. Roger Wicker
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never advanced the bill to a hearing or markup, leaving it without committee action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's sole Independent, with no Republican support, and the Republican-chaired Commerce Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Internet platforms and social media companies
industries.note: These companies' core business is collecting and monetizing user data; the duty of loyalty and restrictions on selling or sharing data would constrain advertising-driven revenue models. The bill's protections run directly against how they currently profit.
Businesses that buy, sell, and resell personal data would need contracts binding them to the same duties and would face liability, sharply limiting the open resale market for personal information.
The bill extends FTC enforcement over common carriers for these duties, closing a jurisdictional gap that currently limits FTC privacy action against broadband and telecom companies.

The FTC may exempt smaller providers based on size, complexity, and cost-benefit factors, easing compliance burdens, though small firms would still face duties until and unless an exemption is written.
